Q001219.stem: A production pipeline must stop after staging until a release manager approves. Approvals must expire if nobody acts within 3 days, the approver must be able to see the staging URL, and only the release-manager group may approve. Which design fits?

choices.text: A Lambda action that sleeps until an approval flag is set in DynamoDB
A CodeBuild step that polls an approval ticket
A Step Functions wait state inserted as a custom action with no timeout
A Manual approval action with SNS and IAM-scoped approvers

Q001219.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodePipeline's manual approval action pauses the pipeline, notifies through SNS, can include a URL for review, and times out after 7 days if not acted on. Here the 3-day expiry can be enforced by a process or custom automation that rejects the approval, while IAM on codepipeline:PutApprovalResult restricts who can approve.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda sleeping: Lambda has a 15-minute limit and isn't a pipeline pause mechanism.
• Step Functions custom action: adds complexity; the built-in approval action already exists.
• CodeBuild polling: wastes build minutes and is fragile.

Key takeaway: human gates in CodePipeline → manual approval action + IAM on PutApprovalResult.

Q001221.stem: An EC2 in-place CodeDeploy deployment must stop the old app gracefully, back up config before files are copied, set permissions after copying, start the app, and then run a health check that fails the deployment if unhealthy. In which hooks do these scripts belong, in order?

choices.text: ApplicationStop, AfterInstall, BeforeInstall, ValidateService, ApplicationStart
ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, ValidateService
DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart
BeforeInstall, ApplicationStop, ApplicationStart, AfterInstall, ValidateService

Q001221.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy runs ApplicationStop first (using the previous revision's script), then BeforeInstall (pre-copy tasks such as backups), then the Install step copies files, then AfterInstall (permissions and config), ApplicationStart, and finally ValidateService, where a non-zero exit fails the deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stop after BeforeInstall: the old app should stop before preparation.
• ValidateService before ApplicationStart: you can't validate an app that hasn't started.
• DownloadBundle and Install: reserved steps run by the agent; you can't attach scripts to them.

Key takeaway: remember the order Stop → BeforeInstall → (Install) → AfterInstall → Start → Validate.

Q001225.stem: A platform stores 15,000 configuration parameters, some 6 KB, read at high rates during deploys. Some parameters must expire automatically after 30 days. Which Parameter Store configuration fits?

choices.text: Standard tier, splitting each 6 KB value across two parameters
Advanced tier with expiration policies
Standard tier, raising the parameter count with a quota increase
Move everything to Secrets Manager, which has no size or rate limits

Q001225.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Advanced parameters allow a higher total count, values up to 8 KB, and parameter policies such as expiration. Higher throughput is a separate account setting for heavy read loads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard tier with a quota increase: standard values are limited to 4 KB, and there's no parameter policy support.
• Splitting values: fragile and still no expiration policies.
• Secrets Manager: costs more per secret and has its own quotas; it isn't meant for plain configuration.

Key takeaway: large values, policies, or high counts → advanced tier.

Q001227.stem: A team wants every merge to main to be releasable, with short-lived branches and no merge hell. It uses GitHub and CodePipeline. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: GitFlow with long-lived develop and release branches, each with its own pipeline
Direct commits to main, with tests run weekly by the QA team
Trunk-based development with required CodeBuild PR checks
Feature branches kept open until complete, then merged without CI

Q001227.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trunk-based development keeps changes small and merges often into main. Required status checks from CodeBuild on pull requests ensure only passing code merges, and each merge triggers the delivery pipeline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GitFlow: long-lived branches delay integration and cause merge conflicts.
• Long feature branches without CI: the recipe for merge hell and broken main.
• Weekly tests: defects reach main long before they're found.

Key takeaway: continuous delivery = small, frequent, verified merges to one trunk.

Q001235.stem: A team wants test pass rates and trends in the console for every build, plus code coverage percentages, without custom dashboards. Its tests produce JUnit XML and a Cobertura XML coverage file. Which CodeBuild feature fits?

choices.text: X-Ray traces emitted from the test runner
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over build logs
Build badges shown in the repository README
Report groups for test and coverage reports

Q001235.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild report groups read test result files (such as JUnit XML) and code coverage files (such as Cobertura or JaCoCo), and show trends across builds in the console when configured in the buildspec reports section.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: you'd parse text and build dashboards yourself.
• Build badges: show only pass or fail status.
• X-Ray: traces requests, not test results.

Key takeaway: test results and coverage in CodeBuild → report groups.

Q001238.stem: After each production deployment, the team wants synthetic checkout transactions every 5 minutes from outside the VPC, failing and rolling back the deployment if latency exceeds 2 seconds. Which design fits?

choices.text: An ALB health check path with a 2-second timeout
X-Ray sampling rules on the checkout service
A CodeBuild project scheduled every 5 minutes running curl
A Synthetics canary alarm on the deployment group

Q001238.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries run scripted user flows on a schedule and publish metrics. An alarm on canary latency or failures can be attached to the CodeDeploy deployment group for automatic rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ALB health checks: test a single endpoint from inside, not a full transaction.
• CodeBuild cron: rebuilds what canaries provide, with no native rollback link.
• X-Ray: observes real requests; it doesn't generate synthetic transactions.

Key takeaway: synthetic user journeys → Synthetics canaries; tie their alarms to rollback.

Q001243.stem: A teammate overwrote the prod tag in ECR, and a deployment pulled the wrong image. The team wants to prevent tag overwrites and deploy an exact image that can't change later. What should it do?

choices.text: Enable tag immutability and deploy by digest
Enable ECR enhanced scanning on the repository
Require that all pushes go through one CodeBuild project
Add a lifecycle policy that deletes untagged images

Q001243.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tag immutability prevents pushing a new image under an existing tag. Referencing images by digest (sha256) guarantees the exact image content that was tested.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scanning: finds vulnerabilities; doesn't prevent overwrites.
• Lifecycle policy: cleans up images; doesn't protect tags.
• One CodeBuild project: a process control that can still overwrite tags.

Key takeaway: immutable tags + digests = reproducible deployments.

Q001245.stem: A company needs monthly golden AMIs with the latest patches and CIS hardening, automated tests before release, and distribution to 3 Regions and 20 accounts. Launch templates must pick up the new AMI automatically. Which solution fits?

choices.text: An Image Builder pipeline with tests and distribution
A Systems Manager Maintenance Window that patches running instances
An ECR lifecycle policy that rebuilds AMIs monthly
A CodeBuild job calling CreateImage and CopyImage on a schedule

Q001245.explanation:
Why this is correct:
EC2 Image Builder pipelines build, harden, test, and distribute images across Regions and accounts on a schedule, and distribution settings can update launch templates with the new AMI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild scripts: reinvent testing, distribution, and sharing.
• ECR: stores container images, not AMIs.
• Patching running instances: mutable updates, not golden images.

Key takeaway: golden images at scale → EC2 Image Builder.

Q001254.stem: An ASG behind an ALB needs zero-downtime releases, a new fleet for each release, validation before traffic shifts, and instant rollback. Which CodeDeploy approach fits?

choices.text: In-place with OneAtATime on the existing fleet
Blue/green with a replacement Auto Scaling group
A launch template update followed by manual instance termination
In-place with AllAtOnce and a quick rollback script

Q001254.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy blue/green for EC2 copies the ASG, deploys and validates on the new instances, shifts ALB traffic, and can keep the old fleet for a set time so rollback just means rerouting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OneAtATime: slow and modifies existing instances, so rollback means redeploying.
• AllAtOnce: causes downtime.
• Manual termination: no automated validation or rollback.

Key takeaway: new fleet + traffic switch + keep the old fleet = blue/green.

Q001258.stem: Two incidents came from servers that drifted after SSH hotfixes, and one rollback took hours because the previous state was unknown. Which deployment pattern prevents both problems?

choices.text: Mutable deployments with a configuration management agent
Immutable deployments from versioned artifacts
Mutable deployments with SSH changes logged in a wiki
Snapshots before every change

Q001258.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable deployments never change running servers. Each release is a new versioned image or artifact on new instances, so every server matches a known version, and rollback means redeploying the previous version.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config management agents: reduce drift but still mutate servers.
• Logged SSH changes: documentation doesn't prevent drift.
• Snapshots: help restores, but in-place changes still drift.

Key takeaway: immutable = known state and fast rollback.

Q001267.stem: A SAM template deployment fails with 'Transform AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 failed'. The team deploys with plain aws cloudformation create-stack. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: It's a CloudFormation transform; add CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND
SAM templates are deployed by the Lambda service and can't be used with CloudFormation
SAM templates must first be compiled to Terraform
The transform runs only in the SAM CLI, so CloudFormation can't process it

Q001267.explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAM is a CloudFormation transform (macro) that expands resources such as AWS::Serverless::Function into standard resources. Deploying a template with transforms through CloudFormation requires acknowledging CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND (typically with a change set).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda deploys it: CloudFormation deploys SAM templates.
• Terraform: unrelated.
• CLI-only: CloudFormation processes the transform server-side.

Key takeaway: SAM = CloudFormation transform; acknowledge auto-expand capability.

Q001273.stem: A legacy OpsWorks Stacks layer must install a monitoring agent automatically on every new instance as soon as it boots, and again after any instance is replaced. Which lifecycle event should run the recipe?

choices.text: Configure
Setup
Deploy
Shutdown

Q001273.explanation:
Why this is correct:
OpsWorks runs Setup recipes when an instance finishes booting, which suits installing agents and base packages on every new instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deploy: runs when an app is deployed.
• Configure: runs on all instances when an instance enters or leaves the online state, meant for updating configuration such as peer lists.
• Shutdown: runs before an instance stops.

Key takeaway: boot-time installs → Setup; topology changes → Configure. (For new work, prefer Systems Manager.)

Q001278.stem: New business-unit accounts must arrive with a standard VPC, mandatory guardrails, org logging, and SSO access, requested through a self-service catalog with no platform-team steps. Which solution fits?

choices.text: Organizations CreateAccount scripts, with a manual guardrail checklist
A Config aggregator that detects new accounts and alerts the platform team
IAM Identity Center permission sets that let each team build its own VPC
Control Tower Account Factory via Service Catalog, plus customizations

Q001278.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Account Factory provisions enrolled accounts with Control Tower guardrails, centralized logging, and Identity Center access, and it's exposed as a Service Catalog product for self-service. Customizations (for example, CfCT or AFT) add the standard VPC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Scripts plus checklist: manual steps and drift.
• Config aggregator: detection only.
• Permission sets for self-build: inconsistent baselines.

Key takeaway: self-service, governed account vending → Account Factory.

Q001291.stem: An engineer must restart a service on 300 instances tagged Role=web right now, 10% at a time, stopping if more than 5 fail, with output saved to S3. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Run Command by tag, with concurrency and error limits and S3 output
An SSH loop run from a bastion host
State Manager association applied to the tag on a schedule
An Automation runbook with approval steps and a CloudFormation stack

Q001291.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Run Command is for ad hoc, one-time actions across a fleet. It targets by tag, supports rate control (max concurrency and max errors), and can send output to S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• State Manager: enforces a desired state on a schedule, not a one-off restart.
• Automation with approvals: meant for multi-step workflows; heavier than needed.
• SSH loop: requires open ports and keys, with no rate control.

Key takeaway: one-off fleet command → Run Command; ongoing desired state → State Manager.

Q001303.stem: An ALB with cross-zone load balancing enabled has 2 targets in AZ a and 8 in AZ b. What traffic share does each target get, and what happens if cross-zone is disabled for the target group?

choices.text: Enabled: each target gets about 10%; disabled: AZ a targets get about 25% each
Enabled: each AZ gets 50%; disabled: each target gets 10%
Cross-zone can't be disabled on an ALB, so each target always gets 10%
Enabled: AZ b targets get 80% total; disabled: traffic stops to AZ a

Q001303.explanation:
Why this is correct:
With cross-zone on, requests spread evenly across all 10 healthy targets (about 10% each). With it off, each AZ's load balancer node sends traffic only to targets in its own AZ, and the nodes receive traffic roughly equally, so the 2 AZ-a targets split about 50% (about 25% each).

Why the other options are wrong:
• 50% per AZ when enabled: that's the disabled behavior.
• 80% to AZ b with nothing to AZ a: disabling doesn't drain a zone.
• Can't disable: ALB allows turning it off at the target group level.

Key takeaway: uneven targets per AZ + cross-zone off = hot targets.

Q001304.stem: A team says, 'S3 Standard has 11 nines, so we don't need Versioning or backups.' Which reply is correct?

choices.text: Correct; 11 nines durability also protects against accidental deletes
Durability guards against hardware loss, not deletes or overwrites
Correct, but only if the bucket is in a Region with three or more AZs
11 nines refers to availability, so outages are the only risk

Q001304.explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3's durability design protects against losing data to infrastructure failure. It doesn't protect against a user or program deleting or overwriting objects, so Versioning, Object Lock, or backups are still needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Protects against deletes: S3 will faithfully delete what you tell it to.
• AZ count: doesn't change the deletion risk.
• Availability: S3 Standard's availability design is 99.99%; 11 nines is durability.

Key takeaway: durability ≠ protection from mistakes.

Q001327.stem: Instances emit session counts every 10 seconds, and alarms must react within 30 seconds. Which approach fits?

choices.text: PutMetricData at standard resolution with 60-second alarms
Agent StatsD metrics at 1-second resolution
Enable EC2 detailed monitoring
Log the counts and create a metric filter

Q001327.explanation:
Why this is correct:
High-resolution custom metrics store data at 1-second granularity and support alarms on 10-second (or 30-second) periods. The CloudWatch agent's StatsD support collects these metrics easily.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standard resolution: 60-second granularity can't react in 30 seconds.
• Metric filters: produce standard-resolution metrics.
• Detailed monitoring: 1-minute EC2 metrics, not custom application counts.

Key takeaway: sub-minute alarms need high-resolution custom metrics.

Q001338.stem: CloudWatch Logs storage costs have grown for a year while daily volume is flat. Logs must be kept 1 year for audit but are queried only in the first 30 days. What fits BEST?

choices.text: 30-day retention plus an S3 archive
Keep Never expire, since CloudWatch Logs compresses old data for free
Set retention to 1 year on every log group
Delete and recreate the log groups monthly

Q001338.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Log groups default to never expire, so storage keeps growing. Short retention keeps the query window in CloudWatch, while S3 (with lifecycle to colder classes) keeps the audit copy for a year more cheaply.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Never expire: that's the cause of the growth.
• 1-year retention: meets audit needs but at CloudWatch storage prices.
• Recreating groups: loses data and breaks references.

Key takeaway: set retention on every log group; archive long-term logs in S3.

Q001349.stem: An RDS for PostgreSQL database's storage sometimes jumps unexpectedly. The team wants no manual resizing but must cap cost. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: A FreeStorageSpace alarm that opens a ticket for a manual resize
Performance Insights, which reallocates storage from idle tables
Multi-AZ, which adds storage during failover
RDS Storage Auto Scaling with a maximum storage threshold

Q001349.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Storage Auto Scaling increases allocated storage when free space runs low, and the maximum storage threshold caps growth to control cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Alarm plus manual resize: the manual work the team wants to avoid.
• Multi-AZ: adds availability, not capacity.
• Performance Insights: analyzes load; it doesn't allocate storage.

Key takeaway: automatic growth with a ceiling → Storage Auto Scaling max threshold.

Q001367.stem: The team wants automatic remediation when AWS announces an issue or scheduled maintenance affecting its own EC2 instances, across 20 accounts. Which design fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Insights on EC2 API calls
Health organizational view with EventBridge rules
Poll the public service health page every minute
Trusted Advisor checks with weekly email

Q001367.explanation:
Why this is correct:
The AWS Health API and events are specific to your resources. Organizational view aggregates them, and EventBridge rules on aws.health events can trigger automation such as Lambda or SSM runbooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public health page: general status, not tied to your resources.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks, not service events.
• CloudTrail Insights: unusual API activity, not AWS service issues.

Key takeaway: account-specific AWS events → Health + EventBridge.

Q001373.stem: Security needs one queryable view of Config compliance across 40 accounts and 3 Regions, including SQL-style advanced queries. Which solution fits?

choices.text: Athena queries against each account's Config delivery bucket
Cross-account roles assumed on demand to call Config APIs
One Config rule deployed manually to each account and Region
An organization Config aggregator, with advanced queries

Q001373.explanation:
Why this is correct:
An aggregator collects configuration and compliance data from all accounts and Regions, and Config advanced queries run SQL-like queries across the aggregated data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena on delivery buckets: possible but requires building and maintaining the pipeline.
• Manual rules: deploy rules, not a unified view.
• Assuming roles on demand: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: organization-wide Config view → aggregator + advanced query.

Q001377.stem: A rule must evaluate S3 bucket public access immediately whenever a bucket policy changes, and also re-check all buckets daily in case a change was missed. Which trigger configuration fits?

choices.text: Both change and periodic triggers
Manual trigger run by an administrator daily
Periodic trigger at the minimum interval only
Configuration change trigger only

Q001377.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config rules can use a configuration change trigger (evaluates when a recorded resource changes) and a periodic trigger (evaluates on a schedule). Using both gives immediate detection plus a daily safety net.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Periodic only: delays detection.
• Change only: misses cases where recording didn't capture a change.
• Manual: not automatic.

Key takeaway: change triggers for immediacy, periodic for completeness.

Q001378.stem: An operations engineer needs a cross-account view of patch compliance for thousands of instances and the ability to open a session or browse file systems on a noncompliant instance from the same console. Which capability fits?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs
Change Manager requests
Parameter Store hierarchies
Patch Manager compliance plus Fleet Manager

Q001378.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Patch Manager reports compliance, and Fleet Manager provides a unified console to view managed nodes and perform actions such as sessions, file system browsing, and performance views.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change Manager: approvals for changes, not fleet operations.
• Parameter Store: configuration values.
• Conformance packs: compliance rules, with no instance management.

Key takeaway: fleet visibility and actions → Fleet Manager.

Q001379.stem: During an incident, the team must find the top error messages across 60 log streams in one log group over 2 hours and see how their counts changed every 5 minutes. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Create a metric filter and wait for new data to accumulate
Open each stream in the console and read chronologically
Logs Insights: filter errors, stats by message and bin(5m)
Download all streams and grep them locally

Q001379.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Logs Insights queries across all streams in a log group for any time range, with filter, stats, and bin() for time-bucketed counts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metric filter: applies only to new data, not the past 2 hours.
• Local grep: slow and manual.
• Reading streams: impractical at this scale.

Key takeaway: ad hoc aggregation over historical logs → Logs Insights.

Q001381.stem: A pipeline's CodeBuild action shows only 'Build failed'. The engineer must find the failing command and also keep logs for 90 days for audits. What should the engineer check and configure?

choices.text: The CodePipeline execution summary, which contains full build output
The artifact bucket, which stores an error file
CodeBuild logs, with 90-day retention
CloudTrail event history, which records compiler errors

Q001381.explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild streams build output to CloudWatch Logs (and optionally S3). Setting log group retention or S3 lifecycle meets the audit period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pipeline summary: shows action status only.
• CloudTrail: records API calls, not command output.
• Artifact bucket: stores artifacts, not logs.

Key takeaway: build output lives in CodeBuild logs; manage their retention.

Q001394.stem: An admin updates the DataAnalyst permission set in IAM Identity Center. Users in 12 accounts still have old permissions. What explains this, and what fixes it?

choices.text: Reprovision the permission set to the accounts
Permission sets apply only to new users; recreate the users
Identity Center caches policies in the browser; clear cookies
Changes take 24 hours to propagate automatically

Q001394.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates an IAM role (AWSReservedSSO_...) in each assigned account from the permission set. After editing a permission set, it must be provisioned to the assigned accounts so those roles are updated.

Why the other options are wrong:
• New users only: assignments aren't user-creation dependent.
• 24-hour propagation: there's no such automatic delay; provisioning pushes changes.
• Browser cache: permissions are evaluated by IAM on the role, not the browser.

Key takeaway: permission set → IAM role per account; reprovision after changes.

Q001396.stem: A custom rotation Lambda for a third-party API key must never leave applications with an invalid key during rotation. Which step order does Secrets Manager call, and where is the new key activated in the vendor system?

choices.text: createSecret, testSecret, setSecret, finishSecret; activate in testSecret
finishSecret first to stage AWSPENDING, then the other steps
setSecret, createSecret, finishSecret, testSecret; activate in finishSecret
createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, finishSecret; activate in setSecret

Q001396.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rotation runs createSecret (generate the new value as AWSPENDING), setSecret (apply it in the target system), testSecret (verify it works), and finishSecret (move AWSCURRENT to the new version). Apps keep using AWSCURRENT until finishSecret, so they're never left with an unusable key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Other orders: CreateSecret must come first and finishSecret last.
• finishSecret first: would promote a value before it exists or is tested.

Key takeaway: create → set → test → finish; staging labels keep clients safe.

Q001399.stem: An SG allows TCP 443 from 203.0.113.0/24, but connections still fail. The subnet NACL has rule 90 DENY 203.0.113.0/24 all traffic and rule 100 ALLOW 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. What is happening?

choices.text: Security groups override NACLs, so the SG allow should win
The NACL's rule 90 matches first and denies the traffic
NACL rules apply only to outbound traffic
NACLs evaluate the most specific rule regardless of number

Q001399.explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs evaluate rules in ascending number order and stop at the first match, so rule 90's DENY wins before rule 100 is considered. Both NACL and SG must allow traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG overrides: both layers must allow.
• Most specific wins: NACLs use rule order, not specificity.
• Outbound only: NACLs have inbound and outbound rules.

Key takeaway: NACL = first match by rule number.

Q001402.stem: Customer export files land in an S3 bucket daily. The company wants alerts within minutes when a file contains card numbers, and wants the finding to trigger automatic quarantine of the object. Which design fits?

choices.text: Config rules that check bucket encryption
Macie jobs; findings via EventBridge to Lambda
Inspector scans of the bucket with automated remediation
GuardDuty S3 Protection findings that trigger quarantine

Q001402.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie classification jobs scoped to new objects detect card numbers, and Macie findings are published to EventBridge, where a rule can invoke Lambda to move or tag the object.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: detects suspicious access, not data content.
• Config encryption rules: encryption status, not content.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities, not data classification.

Key takeaway: content-based alerts on S3 data → Macie findings + EventBridge.

Q001405.stem: During a large DDoS, an ALB-backed service scaled out for hours and the bill spiked. Which Shield Advanced benefit addresses this, and what is required?

choices.text: Discounts on Reserved Instances bought during attacks
Cost protection credits for protected resources
Automatic refunds for downtime on any resource
Free usage of all services during attacks

Q001405.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's DDoS cost protection provides credits for scaling charges on protected resources caused by attacks. The resource must be added to Shield Advanced protections.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Downtime refunds: not part of Shield.
• RI discounts and free usage: not offered.

Key takeaway: cost protection applies only to resources you protect.

Q001410.stem: An auditor needs proof that CloudTrail logs in S3 were not altered or deleted after delivery, and proof that nobody can delete them for 7 years. Which combination fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Lake plus a bucket policy denying deletes
CloudTrail Insights plus S3 Versioning
Config history plus MFA Delete
Log file validation plus Object Lock

Q001410.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Log file integrity validation uses signed digest files to prove files weren't changed or removed. Object Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion for the retention period, even by root.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Insights and Versioning: Insights detects anomalies; versions can be deleted.
• Config and MFA Delete: Config doesn't verify log integrity; MFA Delete can be disabled by the owner.
• Bucket policy: administrators can change it.

Key takeaway: prove integrity → validation; enforce retention → Object Lock.

Q001414.stem: The team wants a page within 5 minutes when more than 10 AccessDenied errors occur from any single IAM principal in CloudTrail logs delivered to CloudWatch Logs. Which approach fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules scanning CloudTrail content
A metric filter with principal as a dimension, and an alarm
GuardDuty, which has a built-in finding for this exact threshold
A daily Athena query over the S3 trail

Q001414.explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metric filters can extract fields such as the principal ARN as dimensions, producing a metric per principal, and an alarm on that metric can page within minutes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty: detects threats with its own logic, not custom thresholds.
• Daily Athena: too slow.
• Config: evaluates resource configuration, not log content.

Key takeaway: custom thresholds on log events → metric filter (with dimensions) + alarm.
